Alternative blending models

v04-alternative-blending-models.Rmd

mixRSMflow: Alternative Blending Models and Parameterizations

Extended instructional vignette
Package: mixRSMflow
Version targeted: 0.1.0.9000
Extended vignette: 26
Format: Markdown source only
Primary ownership: nonstandard mixture-model bases, fixed-exponent General Blending Models, ratio/log-contrast/Cox/slack formulations, Becker families, additive blending, Kronecker basis, segmented surfaces, model reduction and interpretation across parameterizations
Companion material: 05-scheffe-models.Rmd, 06-alternative-mixture-models.Rmd; Extended Vignettes 24 and 25 provide geometry and design

This document is intentionally supplied as .md. It is an extended teaching monograph. Examples emphasize model meaning and numerical behavior rather than automatically selecting a more flexible formulation.

Scope boundary. This extended vignette owns the topic named in its title. Closely related methods that belong to another extended vignette are referenced rather than re-taught. This separation is deliberate so that the extended documentation remains deep without becoming repetitive.

1. Why an extended vignette on alternative mixture models?

Scheffé polynomials are the natural starting point for mixture response surfaces, but they do not exhaust the scientifically useful ways to express blending behavior. Some formulation problems involve ratios, substitutions around a reference composition, a dominant slack component, inverse behavior near small proportions, grouped blend laws, or response regimes that change at a component threshold.

The important question is not “Which formula gives the highest R-squared?” It is:

Which model basis expresses a scientifically plausible blending mechanism over the actually observed mixture region while remaining estimable, stable, and interpretable?

mixRSMflow makes the basis explicit through mix_basis(). This is central to transparent mixture modeling because users can inspect the columns before fitting them.

2. Learning objectives

After this vignette, the reader should be able to:

  1. inspect the exact design/model matrix generated by mix_basis();
  2. use Scheffé models as a reference model space rather than as an automatic final choice;
  3. explain when inverse terms are scientifically plausible and numerically dangerous;
  4. construct component-ratio models and diagnose denominator problems;
  5. interpret Cox coordinates around a declared reference blend;
  6. fit log-contrast models only when all logged components are strictly positive;
  7. choose and explain a slack-variable parameterization;
  8. distinguish Becker H1, H2, and H3 families conceptually;
  9. use additive-blending terms when one component follows a different blending rule;
  10. define fixed-exponent General Blending Model terms with mix_gbm_term();
  11. verify the identity between a special GBM configuration and the Scheffé product x_i x_j;
  12. construct a Kronecker quadratic basis for methodological comparison;
  13. fit segmented mixture surfaces when a pre-specified component threshold defines different regimes;
  14. compare alternative models through prediction, diagnostics, hierarchy, and scientific meaning;
  15. reduce a model without silently changing the scientific estimand;
  16. distinguish reparameterization from a genuinely different model space.

3. Function map

Task Function
Construct a basis explicitly mix_basis()
Fit a response model mix_fit()
Create a fixed-exponent GBM term mix_gbm_term()
Reexpress through a slack component mix_reparameterize()
Fit two regimes across a threshold mix_segmented_fit()
Predict from segmented surface mix_predict_segmented()
Compare fitted candidates mix_compare()
Reduce a candidate model mix_reduce()
Diagnose instability mix_diagnose(), mix_collinearity()
Predict/plot mix_predict(), mix_plot()

The full feasible-region treatment is in Extended Vignette 24. Optimal design for a chosen alternative basis is a separate design problem covered in Extended Vignette 25.

Part I. Start by seeing the model matrix

4. Teaching data and specification 

library(mixRSMflow)

sp <- mix_spec(c("A", "B", "C"))

d <- mix_demo_data(
  "mixture",
  n_rep = 3,
  seed = 26001
)

head(d)

Inspect a few distinct blends:

x <- unique(d[c("A", "B", "C")])
head(x)

5. Scheffé quadratic as the reference basis 

Xq <- mix_basis(
  x,
  sp,
  model = "scheffe_quadratic"
)

head(Xq)
colnames(Xq)

For three components the familiar basis is

[x1,x2,x3,x1x2,x1x3,x2x3]. [x_1,x_2,x_3,x_1x_2,x_1x_3,x_2x_3].

The coefficient values are attached to these constrained basis functions. They are not ordinary slopes from three independent factors.

Fit the reference model:

m_q <- mix_fit(
  "response",
  d,
  sp,
  model = "scheffe_quadratic"
)

Every alternative considered below should be compared with an explicit scientific reference like this rather than with an undefined “default model.”

Part II. Slack-variable models

6. Why use a slack component?

Because

xA+xB+xC=1, x_A+x_B+x_C=1,

one component can be written as a remainder. If C is the slack component,

xC=1−xA−xB. x_C=1-x_A-x_B.

Construct the basis:

X_slack <- mix_basis(
  x,
  sp,
  model = "slack_quadratic",
  slack_component = "C"
)

head(X_slack)

Fit directly:

m_slack <- mix_fit(
  "response",
  d,
  sp,
  model = "slack_quadratic",
  slack_component = "C"
)

6.1 Reparameterize an existing fit 

m_repar <- mix_reparameterize(
  m_q,
  slack_component = "C"
)

m_repar

Interpretation

A slack-variable representation can make a substitution story easier to tell when one material is naturally the balancing carrier. For example, if A and B are two active nutrient sources and C is an inert carrier, increasing A at fixed B necessarily displaces C.

Do not choose the slack component after inspecting coefficient significance. Choose it because the formulation process makes that component a meaningful remainder.

Part III. Inverse terms

7. Construct an inverse-term basis

Inverse terms can express sharp response changes at small component amounts.

x_pos <- x[
  x$A > 0 & x$B > 0 & x$C > 0,
]

X_inv <- mix_basis(
  x_pos,
  sp,
  model = "inverse_scheffe",
  inverse_components = c("A", "B")
)

head(X_inv)

7.1 Scientific interpretation

An inverse component term implies behavior that changes rapidly as a component approaches zero. This may be plausible in examples where a tiny amount of an essential binder, catalyst, stabilizer, micronutrient carrier, or biological inoculant produces a large response difference.

7.2 Numerical danger

If x_i approaches zero,

1/xi→∞. 1/x_i\to\infty.

Therefore:

  • the design must have a strictly positive lower bound for that component;
  • near-zero points can dominate the fit;
  • prediction outside the observed positive range can be extreme;
  • standard errors can become unstable.

7.3 Agronomic example

A seed coating contains a small biological adhesive fraction A. If adhesion fails rapidly below a minimum amount, an inverse-style term may represent the sharp transition more directly than a smooth low-degree polynomial.

This should be a mechanistic hypothesis, not a post-hoc attempt to improve fit statistics.

Part IV. Ratio models

8. Ratios as scientific predictors

Nutrient and formulation science often uses ratios such as N:K, protein:energy, or active:carrier.

X_ratio <- mix_basis(
  x_pos,
  sp,
  model = "ratio",
  denominator = "A"
)

head(X_ratio)

8.1 Denominator choice

The denominator is part of the model definition. Choosing A versus B changes the numerical representation and scientific comparison.

Avoid denominator components that can become zero or extremely small.

8.2 Interpretation example

If A is total N carrier, the ratio B/A can represent a secondary nutrient relative to N. This can have a direct agronomic interpretation unavailable from a generic pairwise product.

8.3 Common mistake

Do not interpret a statistically large ratio coefficient as evidence that the denominator is biologically unimportant. Ratio predictors mix information from numerator and denominator.

Part V. Cox mixture coordinates

9. Reference-blend thinking

Cox parameterizations express movement relative to a reference blend.

ref <- c(A = 0.30, B = 0.30, C = 0.40)

X_cox1 <- mix_basis(
  x,
  sp,
  model = "cox_linear",
  reference = ref
)

X_cox2 <- mix_basis(
  x,
  sp,
  model = "cox_quadratic",
  reference = ref
)

X_cox3 <- mix_basis(
  x,
  sp,
  model = "cox_cubic",
  reference = ref
)

Interpretation

A reference blend can be:

  • a current commercial formulation;
  • a standard fertilizer composition;
  • the geometric center of the feasible region;
  • a formulation chosen before experimentation because it has operational importance.

Do not choose the reference solely to obtain smaller standard errors.

Companion interpretation

Cox component-effect paths are covered in the component-effects material. Here Cox is treated as a model parameterization.

Part VI. Log-contrast models

10. Compositional log contrasts

For positive proportions, log ratios can represent relative composition.

X_log <- mix_basis(
  x_pos,
  sp,
  model = "logcontrast",
  reference = "A"
)

head(X_log)

10.1 Positivity requirement

A logarithm is undefined at zero. If a component is allowed to be absent, an ordinary log-contrast basis cannot be applied without an explicit zero-handling model.

Do not silently add a small constant just to make the code run. That changes the scientific model.

10.2 Interpretation

Log contrasts are naturally interpreted through relative changes. For example, an increase in log(B/A) means B increases relative to A.

This can be scientifically compelling in nutrient balance or compositional chemistry, but it differs from Scheffé blending interpretation.

Part VII. Becker model families

11. H1, H2, H3 bases 

X_H1 <- mix_basis(x, sp, model = "becker_h1")
X_H2 <- mix_basis(x, sp, model = "becker_h2")
X_H3 <- mix_basis(x, sp, model = "becker_h3")

These families provide alternative homogeneous blending structures.

Teaching strategy

Rather than memorizing labels, inspect:

colnames(X_H1)
colnames(X_H2)
colnames(X_H3)

and compare the basis values for the same blends.

Interpretation

Different bases can describe similar fitted surfaces while attaching different meanings and scaling to coefficients. Therefore coefficient tables should not be compared term-by-term across model families as if they were the same estimands.

Part VIII. Additive blending

12. A component with a distinct additive role 

X_add <- mix_basis(
  x,
  sp,
  model = "additive_blending",
  additive_component = "C"
)

head(X_add)

This is useful when one component is hypothesized to contribute in a simpler additive fashion while the remaining components exhibit more complex blending behavior.

Agronomic example

A substrate mixture may combine two biologically active organic fractions while a mineral carrier contributes primarily through a near-additive physical effect.

Again, the hypothesis should be declared scientifically, not inferred only from coefficient significance.

Part IX. General Blending Model

13. Why explicit GBM terms?

The General Blending Model can encompass several familiar mixture terms through fixed exponents.

Create a binary term:

term_AB <- mix_gbm_term(
  components = c("A", "B"),
  g = c(2, 2),
  h = 0.5,
  s = 2,
  label = "AB"
)

term_AB

Use it:

X_gbm <- mix_basis(
  x,
  sp,
  model = "gbm",
  gbm_terms = list(term_AB)
)

head(X_gbm)

For a binary term, the implemented fixed-exponent form is

(xixi+xj)gih(xjxi+xj)gj(1−h)(xi+xj)s. \left(\frac{x_i}{x_i+x_j}\right)^{g_i h} \left(\frac{x_j}{x_i+x_j}\right)^{g_j(1-h)} (x_i+x_j)^s.

14. Recovering the Scheffé cross-product

Set:

gi=gj=2,h=1/2,s=2. g_i=g_j=2,\quad h=1/2,\quad s=2.

Then the term becomes

xixj. x_ix_j.

Check numerically:

term_scheffe <- mix_gbm_term(
  c("A", "B"),
  g = c(2, 2),
  h = 0.5,
  s = 2,
  label = "AB_identity"
)

G <- mix_basis(
  x,
  sp,
  model = "gbm",
  gbm_terms = list(term_scheffe)
)

max(abs(G[, ncol(G)] - x$A * x$B))

This identity is useful as a validation target because it connects the advanced GBM implementation with a known classical basis.

15. Fixed exponents are deliberate

mix_fit() does not silently estimate the nonlinear GBM exponents.

Why?

  • nonlinear exponent estimation changes the optimization problem;
  • identifiability may be weak;
  • standard linear-model inference no longer applies directly;
  • hidden nonlinear estimation would make the basis difficult to audit.

Users explicitly define the exponents or use a dedicated nonlinear workflow outside the ordinary linear fit.

This is a methodological transparency feature, not a missing convenience.

Part X. Kronecker quadratic basis

16. Construct the basis 

X_kron <- mix_basis(
  x,
  sp,
  model = "kronecker_quadratic"
)

head(X_kron)

Kronecker-style models are useful in methodological work and in some combined mixture-process constructions.

The interpretation should follow the explicit basis columns rather than borrowing Scheffé coefficient language automatically.

Part XI. Fit and compare alternative bases

17. A reproducible comparison dataset 

d <- mix_demo_data(
  "mixture",
  n_rep = 3,
  seed = 26101
)

Fit several plausible candidates:

m1 <- mix_fit(
  "response", d, sp,
  model = "scheffe_quadratic"
)

m2 <- mix_fit(
  "response", d, sp,
  model = "cox_quadratic",
  reference = c(A = 0.33, B = 0.33, C = 0.34)
)

m3 <- mix_fit(
  "response", d, sp,
  model = "slack_quadratic",
  slack_component = "C"
)

Compare:

mix_compare(m1, m2, m3, criterion = "PRESS")

Comparison rules

Do not decide from one number. Also inspect:

mix_diagnose(m1)
mix_diagnose(m2)
mix_diagnose(m3)

mix_collinearity(m1)
mix_collinearity(m2)
mix_collinearity(m3)

and compare predicted surfaces over the same feasible region.

18. Prediction equivalence versus coefficient equivalence

Two parameterizations can generate very similar fitted surfaces while producing very different coefficients.

A good comparison asks:

  • Are fitted values nearly identical?
  • Are predictions at scientifically important blends similar?
  • Is one basis more stable numerically?
  • Does one basis answer a clearer scientific question?
  • Does a reparameterization merely relabel the same model space?
  • Does an alternative basis introduce genuinely different curvature or boundary behavior?

This distinction prevents overinterpretation of coefficient tables.

Part XII. Model reduction

19. Start from a larger hierarchical candidate 

m_big <- mix_fit(
  "response",
  d,
  sp,
  model = "scheffe_special_cubic"
)

Reduce:

red <- mix_reduce(
  m_big,
  criterion = "hybrid",
  max_steps = 25
)

red

Compare:

mix_compare(
  m_big,
  red$fit,
  criterion = "PRESS"
)

Interpretation

Reduction is appropriate when the design supports a larger candidate space but the data provide little evidence for all terms.

It is not appropriate to remove lower-order structure that is required for a coherent hierarchical interpretation merely because an individual p-value is large.

Part XIII. Segmented mixture surfaces

20. Why segmentation?

Some blending systems exhibit a pre-specified regime change. Examples:

  • a binder becomes continuous above a critical proportion;
  • a biochar fraction changes water-retention behavior above a physical threshold;
  • a surfactant passes a formulation boundary;
  • a nutrient carrier changes phase or solubility regime.

A single global polynomial can blur that change.

21. Fit two regimes 

d_seg <- mix_demo_data(
  "mixture",
  n_rep = 3,
  seed = 26201
)

seg <- mix_segmented_fit(
  response = "response",
  data = d_seg,
  spec = sp,
  split_component = "A",
  cut = 0.50,
  model_left = "scheffe_linear",
  model_right = "scheffe_quadratic"
)

seg

Predict:

p_seg <- mix_predict_segmented(
  seg,
  interval = "confidence",
  level = 0.95
)

head(p_seg)

Critical safeguard

The cut should ideally be pre-specified from science or investigated under a clearly documented model-selection strategy. Searching dozens of cuts and reporting the best without accounting for selection uncertainty can seriously overfit the surface.

Part XIV. An agronomic ratio-model case study

22. Nutrient-solution formulation

Suppose a nutrient source is composed of:

  • nitrate-dominant source NO3;
  • ammonium-dominant source NH4;
  • organic N source OrgN.

The total N-source fraction is one, but the biological hypothesis focuses on the ammonium-to-nitrate ratio.

sp_N <- mix_spec(
  c("NO3", "NH4", "OrgN"),
  lower = c(0.10, 0.05, 0.05)
)

Create a design before outcomes using the design-focused documentation. After data collection:

set.seed(26301)

dN <- mix_design(
  sp_N,
  type = "simplex_lattice",
  degree = 4
)$data

# Teaching response only.
dN$biomass <- with(
  dN,
  40 +
  5 * log(NH4 / NO3) -
  3 * (OrgN - 0.25)^2 +
  rnorm(nrow(dN), 0, 1.5)
)

Fit a log-contrast candidate:

m_log <- mix_fit(
  "biomass",
  dN,
  sp_N,
  model = "logcontrast",
  reference = "NO3"
)

Fit a Scheffé reference:

m_sch <- mix_fit(
  "biomass",
  dN,
  sp_N,
  model = "scheffe_quadratic"
)

Compare prediction and diagnostics rather than only p-values:

mix_compare(m_sch, m_log, criterion = "PRESS")
mix_diagnose(m_sch)
mix_diagnose(m_log)

Interpretation

If the log-contrast model performs well and the ratio has direct biological meaning, it may be more interpretable than a generic polynomial. If zeros are scientifically possible, however, the log model requires a different treatment and should not be forced.

Part XV. A blending-model decision framework

23. Ask these questions before changing model family

  1. Is the current Scheffé model demonstrably inadequate?
  2. Is there a mechanistic reason for the alternative basis?
  3. Does the design support the new columns?
  4. Are any transformations singular near the observed boundary?
  5. Does the alternative improve prediction at scientifically important blends?
  6. Does it reduce or increase conditioning problems?
  7. Can the coefficients be explained to a domain scientist?
  8. Is the apparent improvement caused by one high-leverage formulation?
  9. Does the fitted optimum remain stable?
  10. Does the model behave plausibly on every feasible boundary?

Part XVI. Common mistakes

24. Using inverse terms with zero components

Do not.

25. Adding a pseudocount to enable log contrasts without saying so

That changes the model and the science.

26. Choosing the ratio denominator after looking at significance

Predefine the scientific ratio whenever possible.

27. Comparing coefficients across different bases as if they had the same meaning

Compare fitted response behavior and model-specific estimands.

28. Estimating GBM exponents implicitly

The current linear workflow uses explicit fixed exponents by design.

29. Selecting a segmented cut only by minimum residual sum of squares

Use scientific justification and account for search uncertainty.

30. Reducing hierarchy until every remaining p-value is below 0.05

Model reduction should combine hierarchy, prediction, design support, diagnostics, and scientific meaning.

Part XVII. Function-selection guide

Scientific feature Start with
Conventional smooth blending Scheffé through mix_fit()
Natural remainder/carrier component slack_* or mix_reparameterize()
Strong behavior at small positive component inverse_scheffe
Mechanistic relative component ratio ratio
Interpretation around a reference blend cox_*
Relative/compositional log interpretation logcontrast
Homogeneous alternative blending becker_h1/h2/h3
Distinct additive role for one component additive_blending
Explicit fixed-exponent blending law gbm + mix_gbm_term()
Specialized quadratic comparison kronecker_quadratic
Predefined response-regime threshold mix_segmented_fit()
Candidate model too large mix_reduce()
Compare candidates mix_compare() + diagnostics

Part XVIII. Reporting checklist

Appendix A. Compact alternative-model script 

library(mixRSMflow)

sp <- mix_spec(c("A", "B", "C"), lower = c(0.05, 0.05, 0.05))
d <- mix_demo_data("mixture", n_rep = 3, seed = 20260813)

m_s <- mix_fit("response", d, sp, "scheffe_quadratic")

m_c <- mix_fit(
  "response", d, sp,
  model = "cox_quadratic",
  reference = c(A = 0.33, B = 0.33, C = 0.34)
)

m_l <- mix_fit(
  "response", d, sp,
  model = "logcontrast",
  reference = "A"
)

mix_compare(m_s, m_c, m_l, criterion = "PRESS")

lapply(
  list(Scheffe = m_s, Cox = m_c, LogContrast = m_l),
  mix_diagnose
)

Appendix B. Boundary with other extended vignettes

This vignette does not re-teach:

  • constrained-region geometry (24);
  • optimal-design criteria and GA search (25);
  • mixture-process randomization structures (27);
  • multiresponse desirability (28);
  • optimum-location bootstrap (29);
  • sequential BO (30);
  • response-family/GLS/mixed/Bayesian engines as a general topic (31);
  • full figure-production standards (32);
  • software validation/release gates (33).

Final perspective

Alternative mixture models are useful when they express a better scientific question, not merely when they fit more flexibly.

A rigorous sequence is:

scientific blending hypothesis -> explicit basis -> design support -> fit -> diagnostics -> predictive comparison -> boundary behavior -> interpretation -> optimization sensitivity.

Appendix C. Advanced alternative-model laboratories

C1. Laboratory: same surface, different parameterization

Fit a Scheffé quadratic model and a slack-variable reparameterization. Compare fitted values at all observed blends.

sp_lab <- mix_spec(c("A", "B", "C"))
d_lab <- mix_demo_data("mixture", n_rep = 3, seed = 261001)

m1 <- mix_fit("response", d_lab, sp_lab, "scheffe_quadratic")
m2 <- mix_reparameterize(m1, slack_component = "C")

p1 <- fitted(m1)
p2 <- fitted(m2)

max(abs(p1 - p2))

Lesson

If fitted values are equivalent, coefficient differences reflect parameterization rather than a new response surface. The methods section should not describe the reparameterized form as empirical evidence for a different biological mechanism.

C2. Laboratory: instability near zero

Create a positive dataset with A values approaching zero. Compare an inverse-term basis and a Scheffé basis.

Tasks

  • inspect maximum absolute basis values;
  • compare condition numbers;
  • remove the near-zero point and repeat;
  • explain why an inverse term can make a single formulation dominate the fit.

The exercise teaches that functional plausibility and numerical stability must be evaluated together.

C3. Laboratory: log-contrast versus ratio model

Use a nutrient system where all components are strictly positive.

Fit:

m_ratio <- mix_fit(
  "response", d_lab, sp_lab,
  model = "ratio",
  denominator = "A"
)

m_log <- mix_fit(
  "response", d_lab, sp_lab,
  model = "logcontrast",
  reference = "A"
)

Compare predictions on a common positive grid and explain the difference between a raw ratio and a log-ratio interpretation.

C4. Laboratory: GBM identity and nonidentity

Create two GBM terms:

t1 <- mix_gbm_term(c("A", "B"), g = c(2,2), h = 0.5, s = 2, label = "AB_Scheffe")
t2 <- mix_gbm_term(c("A", "B"), g = c(2,2), h = 0.5, s = 1, label = "AB_H2")

Compare both columns over the same grid. Identify when the first equals A*B and how the second changes total-degree behavior.

Appendix D. Alternative-model troubleshooting matrix

Symptom Likely cause Response
Inf/huge inverse terms component near zero impose scientifically justified positive bound or reject model
log model fails zero/nonpositive component do not add arbitrary pseudocount silently
ratio model unstable denominator near zero choose scientifically stable denominator or alternative model
Cox coefficients change greatly with reference reference-dependent parameterization report reference and compare predictions
different bases have similar predictions reparameterization/equivalent flexibility interpret model-specific coefficients carefully
GBM basis seems opaque exponents not documented report every g, h, s, label
segmented fit overly good cut selected post hoc account for search/overfitting and justify threshold
reduction removes meaningful hierarchy automatic criterion too aggressive protect lower-order terms scientifically

Appendix E. Guided model exercises

Exercise 1. Basis inspection

Create a five-row mixture grid and print the columns for every model family supported by mix_basis(). Group the bases into polynomial, ratio/log, slack, Becker, and GBM families.

Exercise 2. Reference sensitivity

Fit Cox quadratic models using two reference blends. Compare coefficients and predictions. Explain which quantities are reference-dependent.

Exercise 3. Denominator sensitivity

Fit ratio models with A and B as denominators. Identify the regions where each is numerically unstable.

Exercise 4. Boundary behavior

For a fitted inverse model, evaluate predictions as the inverse component approaches its lower bound. Decide whether the behavior is scientifically plausible.

Exercise 5. Zero challenge

Add one true zero to a log-contrast dataset. Write a methods decision tree for whether to exclude the formulation, choose a different model, or develop an explicit zero-capable compositional model.

Exercise 6. Becker comparison

Compare H1, H2, and H3 basis matrices at vertices, edge midpoints, and centroid. Which terms vanish or persist?

Exercise 7. GBM design implication

Explain why a design adequate for a quadratic Scheffé model may not be optimal for a customized GBM basis.

Exercise 8. Additive component

Choose a component with a scientifically additive role and explain how additive_blending differs from a fully interactive model.

Exercise 9. Segmentation threshold

Propose a physically motivated threshold in a pesticide or substrate example. State how it would be defined before response analysis.

Exercise 10. Predictive comparison

Use mix_compare(..., criterion="PRESS") plus diagnostics to compare three bases. Write a conclusion that does not equate lowest PRESS with proof of mechanistic truth.

Exercise 11. Model-reduction stability

Run reduction from two different starting model families. Compare selected surfaces and optima.

Exercise 12. Reviewer exercise

A manuscript reports “a log-ratio model was superior” but omits zero handling and reference component. Draft a reviewer request for the missing information.

Appendix F. Reviewer-style alternative-model audit

Check whether the manuscript states:

  1. exact basis family;
  2. reference/denominator/slack component;
  3. positivity requirements;
  4. GBM exponents;
  5. cut point for segmentation;
  6. model-selection rule;
  7. design support for every term;
  8. condition diagnostics;
  9. prediction comparison on a common region;
  10. scientific interpretation consistent with the basis;
  11. sensitivity of optimum to model family;
  12. any model gate or implementation limitation.

Appendix G. Interpretation language templates

Ratio model

The response was modeled as a function of relative component quantities with A used as the denominator. Because the denominator was bounded away from zero, the ratio terms remained numerically stable over the experimental region.

Log contrast

All modeled components were strictly positive, allowing log-ratio coordinates to represent relative composition. No pseudocount was introduced.

GBM

The General Blending Model terms were specified with fixed exponents before fitting. Nonlinear exponent estimation was not performed inside the ordinary linear workflow.

Segmented model

The surface was partitioned at the pre-specified A = 0.50 threshold because a physical formulation transition was expected at that composition. Separate model forms were fitted on the two declared regimes.

Model comparison

Candidate bases were compared using predictive performance, conditioning, residual diagnostics, and scientific interpretability; no model was selected from a single p-value or information criterion alone.

Appendix H. Applied alternative-model case bank

H1. Nutrient ratio mechanism

A hydroponic response depends strongly on ammonium relative to nitrate rather than on either absolute fraction in isolation. A ratio or log-contrast basis can match the biological question more closely than a generic quadratic Scheffé polynomial. The denominator must remain safely above zero, and the chosen ratio must be justified before significance is examined. If the ratio model predicts similarly to the Scheffé model but offers clearer biological interpretation, that interpretability can be a legitimate reason to prefer it.

H2. Essential low-dose binder

A coating requires a small binder fraction. Adhesion fails sharply when binder approaches its lower admissible level. An inverse term may reflect this steep behavior, but it also magnifies small numerical errors near zero. The component should have a scientifically justified positive lower bound. The analyst should inspect condition number, leverage, and boundary predictions before accepting the inverse formulation.

H3. Commercial reference formulation

A company evaluates substitutions around an existing product. Cox coordinates can center interpretation around the commercial blend rather than around pure vertices that are never manufactured. The reference should be reported in the original mixture units. Changing the reference can change coefficients while leaving much of the fitted surface unchanged, so reference sensitivity should be understood as parameterization sensitivity rather than evidence of biological instability.

H4. Regime change in substrate physics

Above 35% biochar, water-retention behavior may enter a different physical regime. If that threshold is supported by prior physical knowledge, a segmented surface can represent different response laws on either side. If the threshold is found only by searching all possible cuts, model-selection uncertainty becomes important and the apparently sharp transition may be overfit.

H5. Fixed-exponent GBM for mechanistic blending

A mechanistic formulation hypothesis implies a known homogeneity structure. mix_gbm_term() allows explicit exponents so the basis is transparent. The analyst can verify classical identities and inspect columns before fitting. Hidden nonlinear estimation of exponents would obscure identifiability and change inference, so the package deliberately requires them to be supplied in the ordinary linear workflow.

Appendix I. Short-answer alternative-model review

  1. What is the first diagnostic for an alternative model? Inspect the actual basis columns.
  2. Why are inverse terms risky? They diverge as a component approaches zero.
  3. Why are log contrasts impossible at zero? log(0) is undefined.
  4. Does changing Cox reference change the physical mixtures? No; it changes coordinates/parameter interpretation.
  5. When is a slack model natural? When one component is an operational remainder.
  6. What must accompany a ratio model? The denominator and its admissible range.
  7. What are GBM exponents in this workflow? Explicit fixed inputs.
  8. Is lower PRESS proof of mechanistic truth? No; it is evidence about predictive performance under the comparison.
  9. Why inspect boundary predictions? Alternative terms can behave strongly near zero or constraints.
  10. When is segmentation defensible? When the regime boundary has scientific support or selection is handled transparently.

Appendix J. Deeper conceptual notes on model meaning

J1. Parameterization, estimand, and prediction

Three levels should be separated when comparing mixture models. Parameterization concerns how a given response surface is expressed in coefficients. Estimand concerns what scientific quantity those coefficients or derived contrasts represent. Prediction concerns the fitted response at a composition. Two parameterizations can have very different coefficient tables and nearly identical predictions. Conversely, two bases can look algebraically similar but imply different boundary behavior and therefore different scientific conclusions.

A good model-comparison report therefore presents at least one quantity from each level: the explicit basis, an interpretable effect or coefficient statement, and predicted response behavior over the common feasible region. This is more informative than listing only AIC or R-squared.

J2. Boundary behavior is part of model choice

Mixture optimization frequently pushes fitted surfaces toward edges or vertices. Alternative models that behave innocently in the interior can behave dramatically near zero components. Inverse, ratio, and log terms deserve particularly careful boundary evaluation. Before adopting such a model, create a dense feasible grid and inspect predicted response as each affected component approaches its minimum admissible value. A model that produces implausible divergence within the experimental region should not be retained merely because the global residual sum of squares is small.

J3. Scientific parsimony

Parsimony in mixture modeling is not synonymous with the fewest columns. A model with fewer but difficult-to-interpret singular terms may be less scientifically parsimonious than a slightly larger Scheffé model whose behavior is stable and transparent. Likewise, a mechanistically motivated ratio model can be more parsimonious scientifically even when it has comparable numerical dimension. The decision should balance interpretability, prediction, design support, and stability.

J4. Design dependence

A model family cannot be evaluated independently of the design that generated the data. A ratio or GBM term may be weakly identified if the design never varies the relevant composition contrast. A segmented model cannot estimate both regimes well if only a few points lie on one side of the cut. When an alternative model appears unstable, ask whether the problem is the basis or inadequate experimental support. Extended Vignette 25 explains how the design can be optimized for a declared model basis.

J5. Recommended analysis narrative

A strong manuscript narrative might proceed as follows:

  1. state the classical reference basis;
  2. state the scientific reason for considering the alternative;
  3. define every reference, denominator, slack component, threshold, or GBM exponent;
  4. show that the design supports the basis;
  5. compare diagnostics and prediction on a common region;
  6. interpret the alternative in its own coordinate system;
  7. evaluate whether the practical optimum or decision changes;
  8. retain the simpler or clearer model when improvements are negligible.

This sequence makes alternative-model use auditable and avoids the impression of formula shopping.
